Welcome to the Weekly KAOS — UrbanKaoboy’s end-of-week roundup covering Macro and Geopolitics, where I try and tease out the most impactful bits of the week.

Themes of the Week
The long end ripped to levels last seen before the Global Financial Crisis and the S&P still printed a record, because with the Bond Floor gone the only thing holding the longest-duration names over the canyon is Growth, while a soft jobs print kept Goldilocks on its feet, Oil stayed two-sided, and China pressed on every front at once.

Anyone who grew up on Saturday-morning cartoons knows the moment: Wile E. Coyote sprints off the edge of the mesa, legs still churning, and stays aloft right up until the instant he looks down. That is exactly how the longest-duration corners of this Equity market feel to me as the 30-year grinds toward yields it last touched in 2002 and the 10-year pushes past 5.2 percent, which is the whole argument of the piece I put out last week, Wile E. Coyote Equities and the Vanishing Bond Floor.

The backup in long rates has quietly pulled the implicit Bond Floor out from under valuations, and the only thing keeping the Mag-7 complex suspended over the canyon is the Growth story.

Meanwhile, our untrusty seismograph needle kept jumping all week, with Bessent conceding to the Bond market that the house does not always win, French and Japanese yields punching through multi-decade highs alongside ours,

The cost of consumer credit is rising.

The average interest rate on a US credit card rose +0.2 percentage points in August, to 22.36%, its highest level in 12 months.

This is now only 1.0 percentage point below the record 23.37% set in August 2024.

Since 2021, the average credit card interest rate has surged +6.5 percentage points.

By comparison, the 5-year average before the 2020 pandemic was 14.94%.

Meanwhile, the average interest rate on a 5-year new car loan rose +0.4 percentage points in August, to 7.54%, its highest since August 2025.

This is 3.5 percentage points above pre-pandemic levels, but 0.9 percentage points below its all-time high of 8.4%, recorded in August 2024.

Consumer borrowing has rarely been this expensive.

Why is the White House holding a hearing on Fed governor Lisa Cook now? Trump explained why in July. 

After the Supreme Court let Cook keep her seat while she challenges his attempt to fire her, Trump said on CNBC that the court "sent it back, not based on the merits. They sent it back on process and procedure."

text:
After a wondrous first half for investors, especially for those in growth stocks, the second half of 2026 has been a struggle.  The Russell 3,000 -- which represents roughly 98% of publicly traded US stock market cap -- is up about 3% in the 2nd half, but the average stock in the index is actually down 4.4%.

Along with rising interest rates hurting the most interest-rate sensitive areas of the market, it appears as if the shorts are betting big and winning these days.

We broke the Russell 3,000 into deciles (10 groups of roughly 300 stocks each) based on each stock's short interest as a percentage of its equity float.  We then calculated the average 2nd half percentage change of the stocks in each decile.

Decile one in the chart below all the way to the left of the image, contains the decile of most heavily shorted stocks in the Russell 3,000.  Stocks in this decile are down an average of 13.6% in the 2nd half.  As short interest levels get smaller, performance gets better, and the two deciles containing the least heavily shorted stocks are actually averaging gains in the 2nd half.

During big market rallies, shorts feel the pain and usually push prices higher as they rush to cover.  We're definitely not in that type of environment now, and we haven't been for months.

On the flip side, as the shorts get more confident from their winning ways, the spring gets coiled further.  The next time we get a positive market development that brings investors back into equities, be it

Gas prices first spiked in early 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, then they trended lower for the next few years until they spiked again this year with the US invasion of Iran.

Mortgage rates went from 3% up to 7% during the Fed's massive tightening cycle to address runaway inflation in 2022.  They too had been trending lower over the past few years, but they've moved higher again this year since the Iran War began.

The Financial Times
October 9, 2026

Putting the band back together is surely a great feeling, but a dubious corporate strategy. Starbucks chief Brian Niccol has considered a merger with Chipotle, his $41bn rival — and former employer — the FT reported on Thursday. However neat the match might seem from Starbucks’ corner office, it makes little sense for shareholders.

Niccol knows Chipotle very well indeed. He ran the Mexican-themed restaurant chain for six years before decamping in 2024 to the world’s biggest coffee chain, which was then in a state of considerable disarray. Seen from afar, the two do faintly similar things, serving comestibles to customers who are in a hurry. Both have large, sometimes restive workforces.
Moreover, the ways in which they differ might seem from a distance like opportunities. Chipotle’s balance sheet is free of debt; gearing it up a little could provide low-hanging fruit. And while Starbucks has a sprawling global network, Chipotle has yet to venture outside the US, apart from a smattering of international stores.

US consumer median 1-year ahead inflation expectations jumped +0.3 percentage points in September, to 3.9%, their highest level since May 2023.

1-year inflation expectations have now been at or above 3.0% for 22 consecutive months.

Consumers are bracing for a prolonged period of higher prices.
